children: Broadband provider Brightspeed is in talks with its top creditors about new financing options to help fund the continued build-out of its nationwide fiber network, according to people familiar with the matter.

Apollo Global Management, the company's private-equity sponsor, is looking to raise a private asset-backed securitization facility, which typically ranks highest in repayment order, the people said. The proceeds could pay down some of its first-lien, first-out debt or finance continued expansion of its fiber network, the people said. It is looking to third-party investors or certain existing lenders to provide the financing, the people said. Paul Weiss Rifkind Wharton & Garrison is advising Apollo on the matter, the people said.

A wrinkle is that it remains unclear how much of any new ABS proceeds could be used for capital expenditures rather than repaying lenders. The debt documents require roughly 70% of the proceeds to go toward paying down the first-out debt, though some question whether there is flexibility that could allow a workaround of the prepayment requirement, the people said.
A potential facility would be secured by subscription cash flows from the fiber network Brightspeed is continuing to build, WSJ Pro previously reported.
Brightspeed's debt prices tumbled throughout the month ahead of negotiations with the first-priority secured creditors, who are advised by Gibson Dunn & Crutcher and Moelis, the people said.

Most of the second-priority secured creditors have signed a cooperation agreement designed to keep lenders from cutting side deals with the company, the people said. The pact became formally binding last week. Those creditors are advised by Davis Polk & Wardwell and Centerview Partners, the people said.
The company is advised by Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld and PJT Partners, the people said.
Apollo and Moelis declined to comment. Representatives for Brightspeed, Gibson Dunn, Akin Gump, PJT, Paul Weiss, Davis Polk and Centerview didn't respond to requests for comment.

Brightspeed has raised billions of dollars since Apollo formed it in 2022 to fund the fiber build-out. But the cash-intensive expansion, combined with a heavy debt load, caused it to burn through cash. The transition to the high-speed network was slower than anticipated as Apollo worked through an aging copper infrastructure.
In 2024, Brightspeed completed its first distressed debt exchange, wiping out more than $1 billion of debt and extending maturities as lenders agreed to take a roughly 23% discount on their loans.

The restructuring left Brightspeed with roughly $11 billion of debt, mostly spread across four priority tranches in senior secured debt. Apollo owns the third level and a chunk of the fourth, the people said.

As of the second quarter, Brightspeed's fiber network reached 3.2 million homes. Its more than $1.1 billion of cash on hand will only bring it part of the way toward its target of five million homes, the people said.
